nameStory: The bellflower resin bee gets its name from its strong preference for visiting bellflowers (Campanula species) for nectar and pollen. The 'resin' part comes from its unique building habits - unlike its leafcutter cousins that snip neat circles from leaves, this bee collects sticky plant resins to construct its nest walls.
description: The bellflower resin bee is a medium-sized, solitary bee that's part of the leafcutter and mason bee family, though it's actually a resin-worker rather than a leaf-snipper. Females are noticeably larger than males, with robust, dark bodies built for the hard work of resin collection. These native eastern North American bees are important pollinators that provision individual nest cells for their offspring, each egg getting its own carefully prepared nursery chamber.

idTips.label: Resin-collecting behavior
idTips.description: Watch for bees gathering sticky, amber-colored plant resin or even synthetic materials like caulk or putty - they'll work the material with their mandibles until it's pliable

idTips.label: Bellflower preference
idTips.description: Often seen visiting campanula flowers and other bell-shaped blooms, where they'll disappear deep into the flower cups

idTips.label: Robust build
idTips.description: Medium-sized with a sturdy, somewhat chunky appearance compared to other bees - built like a tiny construction worker

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Overall dark body with minimal light markings, giving them a business-like appearance as they go about their building work

idTips.label: Nest construction sites
idTips.description: Look for nests in hollow plant stems, small cavities, or even human-made structures where they've plastered resin into cell walls

habitat: Found throughout eastern New England in gardens, meadows, and woodland edges where bellflowers and other preferred flowering plants grow. They particularly favor areas with diverse native wildflowers and access to resin-producing plants like conifers or plants with sticky saps. Often spotted around residential areas where they may use both native flowers and cultivated campanulas.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from overwintered pupae in late spring, with females immediately starting to search for suitable nesting sites and resin sources.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you'll most likely observe resin-collecting behavior, nest building, and frequent visits to bellflowers and other preferred blooms. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Activity winds down as the new generation completes development, though some late-season individuals may still be visible on late-blooming flowers.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering as pupae in their resin-lined nest cells, completely inactive and hidden from view.

funFact: In 2013, bellflower resin bees made scientific headlines as one of the first insect species documented using human-made synthetic materials for nest construction - they've been caught red-handed using caulk, putty, and other building sealants as substitutes for natural plant resins!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other dark leafcutter bees in the same genus, but the resin-collecting behavior is a dead giveaway - if you see a bee working with sticky, goopy materials instead of cutting neat leaf circles, you've likely found a bellflower resin bee. Remember: leafcutters cut, resin bees collect goo.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the 'leafcutter bee' genus Megachile, these bees don't actually cut leaves at all - they're in a subgenus called Chelostomoides that specializes in resin work instead. This is a perfect example of how common names can be misleading when applied broadly to related species with different behaviors.
compareHints: Unlike the leaf-cutting members of its genus like the patchwork leafcutter bee, the bellflower resin bee works exclusively with sticky materials and never cuts leaf pieces. It's smaller and darker than the invasive sculptured resin bee, and lacks the golden coloration of the golden-tailed leafcutter bee. The resin-collecting behavior immediately separates it from all the true leafcutters in the Megachile genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the leafcutter bees in its genus that cut neat circular pieces from leaves, the Sculptured Resin Bee collects sticky tree resins and other plant materials for nest construction.
Among New England's leafcutter bees, males of this species are easily distinguished by their notably broad front legs - most other Megachile males have normal-width legs.
Among New England's many Megachile species, the Alfalfa Leafcutter Bee is distinguished by its agricultural associations and widespread management by farmers.

Among New England's many Megachile species, the Flat-tailed Leafcutter's compressed abdomen sets it apart from relatives like the Alfalfa Leafcutter Bee and Patchwork Leafcutter Bee, which have more typically rounded abdomens.
Among New England's leafcutter bees, the Pugnacious stands out for its completely black coloration and larger size - most relatives have some lighter markings or metallic hints.
Compared to other Megachile species, unarmed leafcutter bees are distinguished by the males' lack of prominent facial or leg spines that many relatives possess.

Among New England's many Megachile species, the Golden-tailed Leafcutter Bee stands out with its distinctive golden abdominal hairs, while relatives like the Black-and-gray Leafcutter Bee have contrasting gray and black coloration instead.
